nodes.label: Britain
nodes.full: The maritime and colonial rival: it takes Canada, India and the sugar islands in the Seven Years War, fights France again in the American war, and floods the French market with machine-made textiles under the Eden Treaty.
nodes.src: background — Dull, 'The French Navy and American Independence' (1975); Henderson (1957)

nodes.label: The Eastern Powers
nodes.full: Prussia, Russia and Austria: France reverses a century of policy to ally with Austria in 1756, loses the eastern theatre of the Seven Years War all the same, and can only watch as the three partition Poland in 1772.
nodes.src: background — Scott, 'The Emergence of the Eastern Powers 1756–1775' (1990)

nodes.label: The foreign presses
nodes.full: Geneva, Amsterdam and Neuchâtel: the Spirit of the Laws, the Encyclopédie, the Social Contract and Voltaire's Dictionnaire are all printed beyond France's reach and smuggled back in, defeating the royal censorship.
nodes.src: background — Darnton, 'The Business of Enlightenment' (1979)

nodes.label: Regency of Philippe d'Orléans — and Law's System
nodes.full: Louis XV is five years old — the Regent Philippe d'Orléans rules from Paris (not Versailles), relaxes court formality, and allows John Law's financial experiment; Law's System crashes in 1720, devastating French finances and creating lasting suspicion of paper money.
nodes.src: Regency council records: Archives nationales, série E. John Law's Mississippi Company prospectus (1719): BnF. The crash of 1720: documented in contemporary pamphlets (BnF), police reports (Archives nationales Y). Faure (1977), La Banqueroute de Law: the standard study. The contrast between Regency libertinism and Versailles formality: Saint-Simon's Mémoires (he was present).

nodes.label: Louis XV — le Bien-Aimé to the unloved
nodes.full: Louis XV reigns 59 years — initially popular ('le Bien-Aimé'), he loses the Seven Years War (1756–1763), giving up Canada and most of France's empire; his private correspondence with diplomats (the King's Secret) reveals parallel foreign policy conducted without his ministers' knowledge.
nodes.src: Louis XV's private diplomatic correspondence ('le Secret du Roi'): Archives des Affaires Étrangères, Mémoires et Documents France 1397–2053. Published: Broglie (1878), Le Secret du Roi. The Seven Years War archives: Archives de la Guerre A1. McManners (1998), Church and Society, Vol.II for the religious dimension. Petitfils (2014), Louis XV: the standard modern biography.

nodes.label: Louis XVI — the king who lost the initiative
nodes.full: Louis XVI inherits a fiscal crisis and an Enlightenment culture that questions royal authority — he appoints Turgot, Necker and other reformers, then dismisses them under court pressure; his convocation of the Estates-General in May 1789 inadvertently triggers the Revolution.
nodes.src: Louis XVI's diary (covering 1766–1792): Archives nationales, KK 622 — the famous entry for 14 July 1789: 'Rien' (nothing, referring to his hunting). His appointment of Turgot 1774: Archives nationales. The Estates-General convocation decree 24 Jan 1789: Archives nationales, série AD. Price (2002), Preserving the Monarchy: the standard study of Louis XVI's political decisions.

nodes.label: Assembly of Notables (1787) — the point of no return
nodes.full: Louis XVI and Calonne call the Assembly of Notables to approve a universal land tax (taxing all landowners including nobles and clergy) — the Notables refuse; Calonne is dismissed; Loménie de Brienne fails similarly; Louis XVI is forced to recall the Estates-General; this refusal by the privileged orders to accept fiscal reform is the constitutional point of no return before 1789.
nodes.src: The Assembly proceedings (22 Feb–25 May 1787): Archives nationales, série KK. Calonne's reform proposal: Archives nationales. Harris (1979), Necker: Reform Statesman of the Ancien Régime: the standard study. Hardman (1995), French Politics 1774–1789, ch.9: the standard analysis of the Assembly's refusal. The connection to 1789: the convocation of the Estates-General 24 Jan 1789 is directly documented as a consequence of the Notables' failure.

nodes.label: Maupeou Revolution (1771–1774) — the coup that could have saved the monarchy
nodes.full: Chancellor Maupeou strips the hereditary Parlements of their political power in January 1771 — exiling the judges and replacing them with crown-appointed magistrates; this is the most radical royal consolidation since Richelieu; Louis XVI reverses it immediately on accession (1774), restoring the Parlements' veto power and guaranteeing the fiscal gridlock of the 1780s.
nodes.src: Maupeou's edict January 1771: Archives nationales, série E. The exile of the Parlement judges: documented. Louis XVI's reversal (12 Nov 1774): Gaceta — documented. Doyle (1970), 'The Parlements of France and the Breakdown of the Old Regime', French Historical Studies: the standard analysis. Swann (1995), Politics and the Parlement of Paris under Louis XV: the standard study of Maupeou's coup. The reversal's consequences: explicitly linked to 1788 by Necker, Malesherbes and other contemporaries — documented.

nodes.label: War of Austrian Succession — Fontenoy and the 'stupid peace'
nodes.full: France wins the War of Austrian Succession including Marshal Saxe's brilliant victory at Fontenoy (11 May 1745) — but at the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) Louis XV returns all French territorial gains for no compensation; the popular phrase 'bête comme la paix' (as stupid as the peace) permanently damages his reputation as 'le Bien-Aimé'.
nodes.src: The Battle of Fontenoy 11 May 1745: Archives de la Guerre A1 — Saxe's dispatches. Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (18 Oct 1748): Archives des Affaires Étrangères. The phrase 'bête comme la paix': documented in contemporary pamphlets (BnF). Showalter (2012), The Wars of Frederick the Great: contextualises Fontenoy. The Treaty's impact on Louis XV's reputation: documented in police surveillance reports of public opinion (Archives nationales, série Y) — Arlette Farge's work on these reports.

nodes.label: Seven Years War — France loses its empire
nodes.full: The Seven Years War is France's catastrophic colonial defeat — Canada, most of India and Caribbean islands are lost to Britain; the Peace of Paris (1763) is the greatest colonial contraction in French history to that point; Voltaire mocks Canada as 'quelques arpents de neige'.
nodes.src: Archives de la Guerre A1: French military records. Peace of Paris 10 Feb 1763: Archives des Affaires Étrangères; British National Archives SP 108. The battle of the Plains of Abraham 13 Sep 1759: documented in both French and British military records. Voltaire's 'quelques arpents de neige': Candide (1759), Ch.23. Dziembowski (1998), Un nouveau patriotisme français: analyses French public opinion during the war.

nodes.label: American War of Independence — France's revenge
nodes.full: France enters the American war against Britain in 1778 — Lafayette volunteers, Rochambeau commands French forces at Yorktown; the Treaty of Paris (1783) partially reverses the 1763 losses but at enormous financial cost that accelerates the fiscal crisis leading to the Revolution.
nodes.src: French declaration of war on Britain 17 Jun 1778: Archives des Affaires Étrangères. Rochambeau's Yorktown dispatches: Archives de la Guerre A1. Lafayette's letters: Library of Congress. French debt from the war: documented in Necker's Compte rendu (1781). Dull (1975), The French Navy and American Independence: the standard study.

nodes.label: The Calas Affair — Voltaire and judicial reform
nodes.full: Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant, is judicially tortured and executed in Toulouse on false evidence of killing his son to prevent conversion — Voltaire campaigns publicly for his rehabilitation; the case is overturned in 1765 and becomes the founding moment of European human rights advocacy.
nodes.src: The Toulouse tribunal records: Archives départementales de la Haute-Garonne. The rehabilitation decision 1765: Archives nationales, Conseil du Roi. Voltaire, Traité sur la Tolérance (1763): BnF first edition. Bien (1960), The Calas Affair: the standard study. Voltaire's campaign letters: published in his Correspondence (Besterman edition, 51,000 letters — the largest surviving 18th-c correspondence).

nodes.label: Necker's Compte rendu — public finance made public
nodes.full: Jacques Necker publishes the first public account of royal finances — the Compte rendu au roi (1781) is the first time French fiscal data is shared with the public; it sells 100,000 copies immediately and transforms public debate about royal spending.
nodes.src: Compte rendu au roi (Feb 1781): BnF first edition. 100,000 copies in weeks: documented in publisher's records. Hardman (1995), French Politics 1774–1789: the standard study. Necker's subsequent dismissal and rehiring: documented in Archives nationales. The Compte rendu's reliability: debated by historians — Harris (1979), Necker: Reform Statesman of the Ancien Régime.

nodes.label: Edict of Versailles (1787) — Protestants restored to civil existence
nodes.full: Louis XVI's Edict of Versailles (November 1787) officially restores civil rights to French Protestants — the right to marry legally, register births and deaths, and inherit property; ending over a century of legal non-existence following the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685); a landmark of late Ancien Régime religious toleration.
nodes.src: Édit de Versailles (November 1787): Archives nationales; Gaceta — text published. Lüthy (1959), La Banque protestante en France de la Révocation à la Révolution: the standard study of Protestant civil disability and its end. The practical consequences: Protestant marriage registers begin in 1788 — documented in departmental archives. The Calas Affair connection: Voltaire's campaign (1762–1765) documented as one of the long-term causes of this edict.

nodes.label: Convulsionnaires of Saint-Médard — 'God is forbidden from working miracles here'
nodes.full: Jansenist pilgrims flock to the tomb of Deacon Pâris at Saint-Médard cemetery (1728–1732) — falling into violent miraculous trances (convulsions); the crown closes the cemetery by force in January 1732; the famous satirical graffito follows: 'By order of the King, God is forbidden from working miracles in this place'; the episode becomes a focal point for anti-clerical and anti-royal mockery.
nodes.src: The closure order 27 Jan 1732: Archives nationales. The graffito: documented in multiple contemporary sources and police reports. Kreiser (1978), Miracles, Convulsions and Ecclesiastical Politics in Early Eighteenth-Century Paris: the standard study. The police surveillance reports on the Convulsionnaires: Archives nationales, série Y (Arlette Farge has documented these). The episode's political significance: Voltaire uses it in his anti-clerical writings.

nodes.label: Expulsion of the Jesuits from France — 1762
nodes.full: The Paris Parlement expels the Jesuits from France on 6 August 1762 — 3,000 Jesuits are forced to leave or secularise; it is the most dramatic assertion of Gallican parliamentary power before the Revolution.
nodes.src: Parlement of Paris arrêt 6 Aug 1762: Archives nationales, série X. The Jesuits' response and appeal to the Pope: Vatican Archives (ASV). The royal edict confirming expulsion 1764: Archives nationales. Latreille (1950), L'Église catholique et la Révolution française, Vol.I: the standard study. Spain's parallel expulsion 1767: the two are connected — documented in both French and Spanish archives.

nodes.label: Watteau and the fête galante — Rococo as style
nodes.full: Jean-Antoine Watteau is admitted to the Académie Royale in 1717 with a new genre — the fête galante (elegant outdoor party); his Pilgrimage to the Island of Cythera defines the Rococo aesthetic; he dies of tuberculosis aged 36, leaving only 200 paintings.
nodes.src: Pilgrimage to the Island of Cythera (1717): Louvre (INV 8525). Watteau's Académie reception recorded in: Procès-verbaux de l'Académie Royale (Archives nationales, série O1). The catalogue of his work: Rosenberg & Prat (1996), Antoine Watteau: catalogue raisonné des dessins. His death 18 Jul 1721: parish records Nogent-sur-Marne.

nodes.label: Rameau and the Querelle des Bouffons
nodes.full: Jean-Philippe Rameau's Hippolyte et Aricie (1733) launches French Baroque opera's greatest period — the Querelle des Bouffons (1752–1754) pits Italian against French musical style, with Rousseau championing Italian and Rameau defending French; the debate is a proxy for the Enlightenment's cultural politics.
nodes.src: Hippolyte et Aricie first performance 1 Oct 1733: Opéra records (BnF département de la musique). Rameau's autograph scores: BnF. The Querelle des Bouffons pamphlets (1752–1754): BnF — over 60 pamphlets. Rousseau's Lettre sur la musique françoise (1753): BnF first edition. Anthony (1973), French Baroque Music: the standard study.

nodes.label: Place de la Concorde and Soufflot's Panthéon — Neoclassicism
nodes.full: Gabriel's Place de la Concorde (1755) and Soufflot's Panthéon (begun 1758, completed 1790) represent the neoclassical turn away from Rococo — both built under Louis XV and XVI; the Panthéon becomes the secular temple of the Revolution within months of completion.
nodes.src: Place de la Concorde: extant. Building accounts: Archives nationales, série O1. Soufflot's Panthéon building accounts: Archives nationales. The conversion to secular use Apr 1791: documented in the Revolutionary assembly records. Middleton & Watkin (1987), Neoclassical and Nineteenth Century Architecture: the standard survey.

nodes.label: David — Oath of the Horatii (1784)
nodes.full: Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii (1784) is the political manifesto of Neoclassicism — three sons swear to die for Rome, their women weep; its austere patriotism, civic duty and self-sacrifice become the visual ideology of the coming Revolution; Napoleon later calls it 'the Revolution already in action' (the phrase usually attributed to Beaumarchais's play).
nodes.src: Oath of the Horatii (1784): Louvre (INV 3692). Exhibited at the Salon of 1785 (painted in Rome 1784): Salon catalogue — BnF. Johnson (1993), Jacques-Louis David: Art in Metamorphosis: the standard study. The painting's political reception: documented in contemporary press (Journal de Paris). David received 6,000 livres from the royal Direction des bâtiments — the royal commission documented in Archives nationales, série O1.

nodes.label: Beaumarchais — The Marriage of Figaro (1784)
nodes.full: Beaumarchais's Le Mariage de Figaro is banned by Louis XVI who calls it 'subversive'; its eventual performance on 27 April 1784 is a cultural explosion; the play's biting satire of noble privilege and incompetence is a primary literary assault on the Ancien Régime; Napoleon calls it 'the Revolution already in action'.
nodes.src: First performance 27 Apr 1784: Comédie-Française records. Louis XVI's ban: documented in court records — he said it 'would be necessary to destroy the Bastille' before allowing it. The first edition: Paris, Ruault, 1785 — BnF. Lever (2009), Beaumarchais: the standard biography. Napoleon's phrase: documented in Las Cases, Mémorial de Sainte-Hélène. The play's 68 consecutive performances (a record): documented in Comédie-Française registers.

nodes.label: Montesquieu — De l'Esprit des Lois (1748)
nodes.full: Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws (1748) distinguishes despotism, monarchy and republic; introduces the concept of separation of powers; directly influences the American and French constitutions; put on the Index of Forbidden Books by the Church.
nodes.src: First edition: Barillot, Geneva, 1748 (2 vols): BnF. The Spirit of the Laws's influence on the US Constitution: Madison's Federalist No.47 quotes it explicitly. On the Index: documented in Vatican records. Shackleton (1961), Montesquieu: A Critical Biography: the standard study. The manuscript: Bibliothèque de Bordeaux.

nodes.label: Diderot and d'Alembert's Encyclopédie
nodes.full: The Encyclopédie ou Dictionnaire raisonné (28 volumes, 1751–1772) is the collective mind of the Enlightenment — 74,000 articles by 142 contributors including Voltaire, Rousseau and Montesquieu; it is banned twice and circulates clandestinely; the primary intellectual monument of the 18th century.
nodes.src: First edition: Paris, Le Breton, 1751–1772 (17 text vols + 11 plates vols): BnF holds complete sets. The ban of 1759: Archives nationales. The ARTFL Encyclopédie Project (University of Chicago): digitised full text. Wilson (1972), Diderot: the standard English biography. The contributor list and article attributions: documented in the project's scholarly apparatus.

nodes.label: Physiocracy — Quesnay's Tableau Économique (1758)
nodes.full: François Quesnay's Tableau Économique (1758) is the first systematic diagram of economic flows — founding Physiocracy, which argues agricultural land is the sole source of real wealth and advocates laissez-faire economics; it directly influences Turgot and Adam Smith; the Physiocrats are the first self-conscious 'school' of economic thought in European history.
nodes.src: Tableau Économique (first version 1758, printed at Versailles by Louis XV himself — 3 copies only): BnF holds a copy. Quesnay's Encyclopédie articles (1756–1757): his earlier economic thought. Meek (1962), The Economics of Physiocracy: the standard English study. Adam Smith's acknowledgment of Quesnay's influence: Wealth of Nations Book IV ch.9. Turgot's Réflexions sur la formation et la distribution des richesses (1766): the direct Physiocratic policy application.

nodes.label: Rousseau — Du Contrat Social (1762)
nodes.full: Rousseau's Social Contract opens with 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' — the founding text of modern democratic theory; banned in France and Geneva immediately; its concept of the 'general will' directly shapes the French Revolution's ideology.
nodes.src: Du Contrat Social: Marc-Michel Rey, Amsterdam, 1762; BnF. Banned by Paris Parlement 11 Jun 1762 (same session as Émile): Archives nationales, série X. The manuscript: Bibliothèque de Neuchâtel. Masters (1968), The Political Philosophy of Rousseau: the standard analytical study. The Social Contract's influence on the Revolution: Schama (1989), Citizens, throughout.

nodes.label: Voltaire's Philosophical Dictionary (1764)
nodes.full: Voltaire publishes the Dictionnaire philosophique portatif (1764) — 118 articles attacking religious intolerance, superstition and arbitrary power in alphabetical form; small enough to hide in a pocket ('portatif'); the most widely distributed Enlightenment text after the Encyclopédie.
nodes.src: First edition: Geneva, 1764; BnF. Voltaire's 51,000-letter correspondence: Besterman edition (Geneva 1953–65) — the largest surviving 18th-century correspondence corpus. Voltaire's papers: BnF and Institut et Musée Voltaire, Geneva. Gay (1959), Voltaire's Politics: the standard study. The Dictionnaire's multiple revised editions (Voltaire kept updating it): documented in bibliographic records.

nodes.label: The royal debt crisis — anatomy of fiscal collapse
nodes.full: France spends the 18th century in escalating fiscal crisis — Law's crash (1720), seven wars, and Versailles maintenance; by 1788 debt service consumes 62% of state revenue; Louis XVI's inability to tax the nobility or clergy makes bankruptcy inevitable.
nodes.src: Necker's Compte rendu (1781): the primary public document. Calonne's reform proposals 1786: Archives nationales, série E. The Assembly of Notables rejection 1787: Archives nationales. Hardman (1995), French Politics 1774–1789: synthesises the fiscal evidence. Bairoch (1997), Victoires et déboires: comparative European fiscal data.

nodes.label: Eden Treaty (1786) — British textiles flood France
nodes.full: The Eden Treaty (Anglo-French free trade, 26 September 1786) lowers tariffs between Britain and France — cheap machine-made British textiles flood the French market, devastating the textile industries of Rouen and Lyon; mass urban unemployment results just before the harvest failures of 1788; the treaty is a direct economic catalyst for the social crisis preceding the Revolution.
nodes.src: Eden Treaty 26 Sep 1786: Archives des Affaires Étrangères; British National Archives. The textile impact: documented in the Rouen and Lyon Chambres de Commerce reports (Archives départementales). Crouzet (1964), 'Wars, Blockade and Economic Change in Europe 1792–1815', Journal of Economic History: contextualises the treaty. Henderson (1957), 'The Anglo-French Commercial Treaty of 1786', Economic History Review: the standard analysis. The unemployment figures: documented in pre-revolutionary police reports (Archives nationales, série F12).

nodes.label: The salonnières — women as the infrastructure of the Enlightenment
nodes.full: The French Enlightenment is organised through salons hosted by women — Marie Thérèse Rodet Geoffrin finances the Encyclopédie; Julie de Lespinasse manages d'Alembert's correspondence; Suzanne Necker's salon launches her husband's political career; the salonnières are the primary intellectual infrastructure of the period.
nodes.src: Madame Geoffrin's correspondence: Bibliothèque de l'Institut de France. Her financial support of the Encyclopédie: documented in Diderot's correspondence. Julie de Lespinasse's letters: BnF (published 1809). Madame du Deffand's 800-letter correspondence with Horace Walpole: Lewis (1939–1980), Yale Walpole Correspondence. Goodman (1994), The Republic of Letters: A Cultural History of the French Enlightenment: the standard study.

nodes.label: Saint-Domingue — the most profitable colony in history
nodes.full: By the 1780s Saint-Domingue (Haiti) produces 40% of Europe's sugar and 60% of its coffee — on the labour of 500,000 enslaved Africans; it is the most profitable colony in the Atlantic world; the enslaved population outnumbers the free population 10 to 1.
nodes.src: Saint-Domingue plantation records: ANOM (Aix-en-Provence). Population statistics: Census of Saint-Domingue 1789 (500,000 enslaved, 32,000 white colonists, 28,000 free people of colour): Archives nationales, Colonies G1. Dubois (2004), Avengers of the New World: analyses the data. The colony's trade value: documented in Chambre de Commerce de Marseille records.

nodes.label: The Diplomatic Revolution of 1756
nodes.full: France reverses its century-long alliance with Prussia and makes peace with Austria (Treaty of Versailles, 1 May 1756) — the 'Diplomatic Revolution' reorganises European alliances before the Seven Years War; it is the most dramatic single diplomatic shift of the 18th century.
nodes.src: Treaty of Versailles 1 May 1756: Archives des Affaires Étrangères (La Courneuve). Kaunitz's role in negotiating the reversal: Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, Vienna. Scott (1990), The Emergence of the Eastern Powers 1756–1775: the standard study. The reversal's irony — France now defending the Habsburgs — noted by all contemporary observers including Frederick the Great.

nodes.label: First Partition of Poland (1772) — France's geopolitical demotion
nodes.full: Prussia, Russia and Austria partition Poland between them without France being able to intervene — demonstrating France's demotion from 'arbiter of Europe' to passive spectator; Poland was a traditional French client state; the partition reveals the shift of European power toward the eastern monarchies and deeply bruises French national prestige under Louis XV.
nodes.src: Partition treaty 5 Aug 1772: documented in the state archives of all three powers. France's inability to respond: documented in diplomatic correspondence (Archives des Affaires Étrangères). Lord (1915), The Second Partition of Poland: the standard study with primary source analysis. Scott (1990), The Emergence of the Eastern Powers 1756–1775: the standard analysis of France's geopolitical demotion. The connection to the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756: the Austrian alliance that was supposed to solve this problem demonstrably failed.

nodes.label: Enfants Trouvés — one-third of Parisian births abandoned
nodes.full: By the 1770s, nearly one-third of all children born in Paris are abandoned at the Hôpital des Enfants-Trouvés — where first-year mortality exceeds 80%; extreme urban poverty and illegitimacy drive the crisis; Rousseau himself abandons his five children to this hospital (documented); the institution is the structural evidence for the Ancien Régime's failure to provide for its poorest.
nodes.src: Enfants-Trouvés admission registers: Archives de l'Assistance Publique — Hôpitaux de Paris (APHP). The abandonment statistics: documented in Dupâquier (1988), Histoire de la population française Vol.II. The 80%+ first-year mortality rate: documented in Hufton (1974), The Poor of Eighteenth-Century France: the standard study. Rousseau's abandonment of his five children: documented in his own Confessions (1782–1789) — a primary source for the practice's social normalisation. The Enfants-Trouvés: the single most damning primary source for Ancien Régime social failure.

nodes.label: Madame de Pompadour — political power through the king's favour
nodes.full: Jeanne-Antoinette Poisson (Madame de Pompadour) is Louis XV's official mistress from 1745 — she appoints and dismisses ministers, directs foreign policy, patronises Voltaire and the philosophes, and commissions the Sèvres porcelain factory; her correspondence is a primary source for political decision-making.
nodes.src: Pompadour's correspondence: BnF fonds français. Her role in the Diplomatic Revolution 1756: argued by Lever (2003), Madame de Pompadour using Affaires Étrangères archives. The Sèvres commission: Manufacture nationale de Sèvres archives. Her apartments at Versailles: Château de Versailles archives. She outlasted all rival mistresses (1745–1764) through political skill documented in multiple sources.

nodes.label: François Mackandal and marronage — enslaved resistance in Saint-Domingue
nodes.full: François Mackandal, an enslaved African in Saint-Domingue, leads a major poisoning conspiracy (1751–1757) targeting white colonists and their animals — documented in the plantation and court records; he organises the maroon (escaped slave) communities in the mountains; executed by burning in January 1758; the first documented large-scale enslaved resistance in Saint-Domingue before the 1791 revolution.
nodes.src: Mackandal's trial and execution January 1758: Archives nationales, Colonies F3 — the primary judicial documentation. The maroon communities: documented in colonial police records (ANOM). Geggus (2002), Haitian Revolutionary Studies, ch.3: uses the ANOM archive. Fick (1990), The Making of Haiti: the standard modern study. Moreau de Saint-Méry's description of the execution: published in his Description de la partie française de l'Isle Saint-Domingue (1797) — an eyewitness account.
